figure_assets.label: Figure 1
figure_assets.caption_text: Figure 1. Illustration of the “Thinking with Images” frame- work. Ideally, “Thinking with Images” models leverage tools or code to generate interleaved images that facilitate visual reasoning tasks. This example demonstrates a successful reasoning trajectory where the model employs a zooming tool to resolve the query.

figure_assets.label: Table 1
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 1. Ablation study of interleaved images within the visual CoT of “Thinking with Images” models. All results are obtained using VLMEvalKit (Duan et al., 2024). The values in parentheses indicate the performance difference compared to the full model.

figure_assets.label: Table 2
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 2. Results on HRBench (Wang et al., 2025c). Qwen3-VL denotes the Qwen/Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct checkpoint. ∆denotes the performance difference. The raw performance is reproduced by us, while the “Thinking with Images” result is reported by the official technical report of Qwen3-VL. We only report HRBench since the reproduced results of other benchmarks are not available.

figure_assets.label: Table 2
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 2. We use Lmms-eval (Zhang et al., 2024) as the evaluation framework as suggested by the Qwen3VL team. The result shows that Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct per- forms similarly, if not better, on perception benchmarks, which aligns with our previous findings for “Thinking with Images”-only VLMs. However, we would like to emphasize that this does not imply that training “Thinking with Images” models is without merit. The goal of this paper is to high- light that performance gains may not necessarily stem from the interleaving of images and text. Further experimentation

figure_assets.label: Figure 2
figure_assets.caption_text: Figure 2. Attention maps of “Thinking with Images” models. We visualize the attention heatmaps on both the input and interleaved images, indicating the spatial focus of the answer tokens. These scores are computed using attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema, 2020). Note that the generation sequence proceeds as follows: Thought text, followed by the interleaved image, and finally the Answer text.

figure_assets.label: Table 3
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 3. Effectiveness of vanilla SFT. DeepEyes-7B is the “Think- ing with Images” model trained by Zheng et al. (2026) that depends on long CoT with tool-generated interleaved images. DeepEyes- SFT-7B is trained by us using vanilla SFT, without reasoning traces or interleaved images. Both models are finetuned from the same backbone, Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b). ∆reports the performance difference between DeepEyes-SFT-7B and DeepEyes- 7B. Avg. denotes the macro average of the 8 benchmarks. The performance gap on MME-RealWorld-Lite (Zhang et al., 2025d) likely stems from its stringent reasoning requirements, for which RL proves more effective than SFT.

figure_assets.label: Table 4
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 4. Results on V∗(Wu & Xie, 2024) with masked images. We mask the regions containing the target object in each image. “Attribute” denotes the attribute recognition task, and “Spatial” denotes the spatial relationship task.

figure_assets.label: Table 1
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 1, are easy to implement, as one need only sup- press the output of the tool/code. This approach is also cost-effective, requiring only inference adjustments. The genuine utility of interleaved images is validated only when their removal leads to a consistent drop in performance.

figure_assets.label: Table 5
figure_assets.caption_text: Table 5. Results on V∗(Wu & Xie, 2024) combining VLMs with Hide (Liu et al., 2025a). “Better context” refers to augmenting visual evidence while avoiding additional textual context, and “Better prior” denotes finetuned priors. Best results are bold.
